title: Editor overview
text: Level editor asge-editor is a native ImGui-based editor for authoring ASGE scenes visually: place and configure entities, wire up components, manage textures, animations and audio, and organise a project's scenes, without hand-writing TOML. It is a plain executable built from the same CMake tree as the engine. Native installers for Windows ( .exe ), Linux ( .deb ) and macOS ( .dmg ) ship with every tagged release: see Releases . Build from source build just the editor Copy cmake --preset windows-editor-debug cmake --build --preset windows-editor-debug --target asge-editor # binary lands at bin/Debug/asge-editor.exe The editor never links against or depends on Game / IGameState : it drives asge::ecs::Registry , SceneManager , AssetManager and IRenderer directly. See Getting Started for the full build setup. Guide Create a project Create or open a project and save its scenes from the File menu. Work with scenes Switch between a project's scenes, spot unsaved changes and rename a scene. Navigate the viewport Move entities, pan, zoom and set up the reference grid. Configure the game window Set the target game window size and preview what each camera frames. Add entities and components Create entities, edit their components in the Inspector and organise them in a hierarchy. Arrange the UI Create buttons, labels, checkboxes, sliders and panels and let a panel lay them out. Import and inspect assets Mount asset folders, load assets and preview them in the Asset Inspector. Add a collider Attach a Collider and draw its rect or circle directly on the viewport. Animate a sprite Slice a spritesheet into a clip and play it with an Animation component. Make an entity follow a path Author PathFollow waypoints by clicking on the viewport and preview the spline.

title: Create a project
text: Create a project A project is the durable unit; a scene is one of its levels. Everything project- and scene-related lives under the File menu. Steps Choose File → New → Create a Project... . Enter a name and a folder, the grid spacing and the game window size. Confirm. The editor creates the project and saves an Empty Scene inside it. Result: an .asgeproject file plus one .asgescene , both open in the editor. File menu reference Item What it does New → Create a Project... Name, folder, grid spacing and game window size; auto-creates and saves an "Empty Scene". New → Create a Scene... Adds a new scene to the current project (disabled without one). Save / Ctrl+P Saves only the project file (mounts, assets, view, scene list) - never scene data, even a dirty scene. Save As... Copies the project and every scene file to a new folder. Save Scene / Ctrl+S Saves the active scene's entities. Open... / Open Scene... Opens an existing .asgeproject / adds an existing .asgescene to the current project. Every scene-affecting item is disabled while no project is open, and scene-specific ones stay disabled until a scene is active: there is nowhere for a new entity or asset import to persist to otherwise. What is stored where .asgeproject - VFS mounts, known asset paths, view settings (grid spacing, target game window size) and the list of scene files. .asgescene - a plain TOML file with one level's entities, the same format SceneManager::SaveScene/LoadScene use anywhere in the engine. asge.session - remembers which project and scene were active; auto-saved every 30 seconds and restored on the next launch. It lives in your per-user data folder ( %APPDATA%\ASGE\Editor on Windows), not next to the executable, so it works when the editor is installed somewhere read-only such as C:\Program Files . Next: Work with scenes .

title: Work with scenes
text: Work with scenes A project can hold many scenes; the editor keeps exactly one active at a time. Steps Find the HUD panel next to the viewport's mouse-position readout. It shows Project: <name> and a Scene dropdown listing every scene the project knows about. Pick another scene. If the current one has unsaved changes (a filled dot next to the dropdown), it is saved first. To rename the active scene, use the Scene panel. This moves its .asgescene file on disk to match; no copy is left behind under the old name. Result: selection, dirty state and asset resolution are reset for the incoming scene. How switching works SceneManager keeps one scene's entities live at a time. Switching away suspends the outgoing scene into an in-memory snapshot instead of destroying it, and switching back to a visited scene restores that snapshot instead of re-reading from disk. Repeat switching is fast and a stale scene's entities never bleed into rendering, picking or the entity list. Previous: Create a project · Next: Navigate the viewport .

title: Navigate the viewport
text: Navigate the viewport The viewport is a real, resizable window with the engine's own camera and viewport math underneath, so every overlay pans and zooms exactly like the scene. Input Effect Left-drag Move the clicked entity (or drag a gizmo arm to constrain to one axis). Middle-drag Pan the camera. Scroll Zoom, anchored on the point under the cursor. Restore View Reset pan and zoom to the default. Set the grid spacing Open View → Grid (disabled without a project). Set the world-space spacing between the reference grid lines drawn behind every sprite. The value is saved in the project's own [View] settings, not in scene data. Previous: Work with scenes · Next: Configure the game window .

title: Configure the game window
text: Configure the game window Tell the editor what size a real build of the game runs at, so the previews match. Steps Open View → Game Window (disabled without a project). Set the target width and height. They are saved in the project's [View] settings. Previews Every entity with a Camera component gets a live preview box: a world-space rectangle showing exactly what that camera frames at the configured game window size, centred on the entity's visual midpoint (its sprite's bounds, not just its transform's corner) at that camera's zoom. It uses the same math as systems::CameraSystem at runtime but is never applied to the editor's own view. A separate preview anchored at the world origin shows the letterboxed game window itself, regardless of any camera, dimming everything outside it like a real letterbox. Previous: Navigate the viewport · Next: Add entities and components .

title: Add entities and components
text: Add entities and components Every entity in the active scene is listed on the right; click one, or click it in the viewport, to edit it live in the Inspector. Steps Click Create Entity in the Entities panel (or Create UI Element , see Arrange the UI ). Select it. The Inspector shows one collapsible section per component the entity has. Use Add Component to attach more. Edit fields directly: there is no intermediate copy and no Apply step. The trailing x on a section removes that component. Duplicate copies the entity with everything under it into the same parent; Delete removes just that entity and its children become roots. Component types A fixed, explicit set rather than generic reflection; each has a hand-written editor next to its Serializer<T> . Component Fields Name / Transform Display name; position, rotation, scale. Sprite Virtual texture path (picked from known assets, not typed), layer, Y-sort. Collider Rect or circle shape, drawable on the viewport: Add a collider . Camera Zoom and follow-smoothing; previewed live in the viewport. AudioSource Clip path (picked from known audio), volume, loop. Animation Clip path, frame duration and a Play/Stop button. It starts stopped so nothing auto-plays when added. PathFollow Waypoints authored on the viewport: Make an entity follow a path . Velocity / Rigidbody Plain physics data: linear velocity, mass and drag. RenderInfo Layer, Y-sort, screen space and sort inheritance. Added automatically, once, whenever a Sprite is. UI components UIRect, UIButton, UILabel, UICheckbox, UISlider, UIPanel and UILayoutItem. Parent entities The Entities panel is a tree: roots at the top level, children nested behind a collapsible arrow. A selected child shows a read-only Parent line. A child's transform is relative to its parent, so moving the parent moves everything under it. Action How New Child Right-click a row: creates a new entity with just a Transform, attached under that row. Detach Right-click a child row to make it a root a

title: Arrange the UI
text: Arrange the UI Build HUDs and menus without writing TOML. Widgets are assembled through the same ui::Create* functions a game uses, so what you see is what a game gets. Create a widget Click Create UI Element in the Entities panel (disabled until a project is open). Pick a type, then fill in its details. Back returns to the type list; Discard closes without creating. In the Panel Parent section at the end of every form, choose a panel (default (none) ) to create the widget as that panel's child. A panel can parent another panel, which is how you nest layouts. Type Settings Button Name, position, size, enabled flag, Color / Hover / Pressed colours, optional caption. Label Text, font, size, alignment and colour. Auto Size fits the rect to the text; turn it off for a fixed size. Checkbox Box colours, the check colour and whether it starts checked. Slider Min, Max and starting Value, the track colour and the thumb's Color / Hover / Pressed colours. Panel Background and border colours, margin, padding, spacing and a layout for its children. Every type also takes a Name, a Position and a Screen Space flag (on by default, so HUD elements stay put while the viewport pans and zooms). Fonts are picked from those loaded in the Assets panel. Afterwards each widget's components appear as Inspector sections (UIRect, Interactable, UIButton, UILabel, UICheckbox, UISlider, UIPanel) without an x : delete the whole entity instead. You can also drag an entity's row onto a panel in the Entities tree to move it in later. Panel layouts A panel's Layout decides where its children go, applied live in the viewport. Layout Behaviour Absolute Children keep whatever position and size they have. Grid (Rows, Columns) Equal cells, filled row by row in sibling order. VStack (Rows) Equal-height rows, each as wide as the panel, top to bottom. HStack (Columns) Equal-width columns, each as tall as the panel, left to right. Slots sit inside the panel's rect, inset by its Margin and Padding, with Spacing

title: Import and inspect assets
text: Import and inspect assets Assets are addressed by virtual path everywhere in ASGE. The editor gives you a panel for the mounts that back those paths and one for browsing what they resolve to. Steps In the Virtual File System panel, add a mount (a virtual root pointing at a real directory) with the native folder picker. In the Assets panel, use Load Asset... to bring in a texture, animation clip, audio clip or .ttf font. The panel lists everything the editor knows about: assets some entity references, plus those you loaded explicitly (so an unused import still shows up). Click an entry to open the Asset Inspector : absolute path, mountpoint and file size, plus a preview for the kind. Kind Preview Texture Pixel dimensions and a scaled thumbnail. Audio clip Duration, size, and working Play/Pause and Rewind controls. Animation clip Every FrameTable field plus a live, cycling preview of its sliced frames. Font A sample string rendered with the font's own glyph metrics. Fonts feed a label's Font Path; changing a label's font size re-bakes it. Next: Animate a sprite turns a spritesheet texture into a playable clip.

title: Add a collider
text: Add a collider Collider shapes get their own viewport interaction mode instead of raw number fields. Steps Select an entity and add a Collider from Add Component . Pick the shape in the Collider Shape dropdown ( Rect or Circle , default Rect). The editor remembers each shape's own last dimensions per entity, so switching back and forth loses neither. Click Draw Collider , then press to anchor the shape and drag to grow it: a rect defines opposite corners, a circle's drag sets its radius from the anchor. Release to commit; Esc restores the previous shape. Reset Collider zeroes the current shape's dimensions. Drawing edits the live Collider component, so the translucent overlay every collider already has shows it updating in real time. Previous: Arrange the UI · Next: Animate a sprite .

title: Animate a sprite
text: Animate a sprite Turn a spritesheet into something an Animation component can play, without an external tool or hand-written TOML. Steps Open the spritesheet texture in the Asset Inspector and click Create Clip . In the modal, set Rows and Columns . A bigger thumbnail shows a live grid overlay and the computed per-cell pixel size. Click Apply . The editor writes <image>_clip.toml next to the texture (creating or overwriting it), then registers and selects it as a new animation clip. Add an Animation component to an entity, choose the clip path and frame duration, and press Play . A clip records which texture it slices ( m_OriginAsset ), so once one exists the texture's button becomes Open Clip and jumps straight to it. Importing a .toml by hand via Load Asset... that doesn't identify its own texture this way is rejected rather than imported half-configured. Previous: Add a collider · Next: Make an entity follow a path .

title: Make an entity follow a path
text: Make an entity follow a path A PathFollow's waypoints are placed on the viewport rather than typed as numbers. Steps Add a PathFollow component to the entity. Click Select Waypoints in its Inspector section. The viewport becomes a click-to-place surface. Edit the path with the mouse, then click End Selection to commit and leave the mode. Input Effect Click Append a waypoint at the cursor's world position. Drag a point Move it (a fixed screen-pixel pick radius, so it is grabbable at any zoom). Right-click a point Remove it. Esc Discard everything placed this session, restoring what was there before. End Selection Commit and exit the mode. Waypoints stay visible as pin markers after selection ends. Outside edit mode, a real Catmull-Rom curve, the same interpolation PathFollowingSystem uses at runtime, overlays the straight point-to-point lines, sampled at the component's own Resolution , so it previews the path the entity will actually follow. Previous: Animate a sprite .

title: Getting Started
text: Installation Build ASGE from source ASGE builds a static library target and installs a CMake package config, so it can be consumed as a subdirectory, via FetchContent , or as an installed package. Prerequisites A C++23 compiler — MSVC on Windows, GCC/Clang on Linux, Clang on macOS CMake ≥ 3.31 Git Clone the repository shell Copy git clone https://github.com/lmriccardo/a-simple-game-engine.git asge cd asge Fetch vendored dependencies SDL3 and the stb single-header libraries aren't pulled in by CMake — a script vendors them per platform. Windows (PowerShell) Linux / macOS Windows (PowerShell) Copy ./scripts/install-deps.ps1 Linux / macOS Copy ./scripts/install-deps.sh Configure, build and test Using one of the provided CMake presets (also buildable without a preset via plain cmake -S . -B build ): Windows Linux macOS Windows Copy cmake --preset windows cmake --build --preset windows ctest --preset windows-debug Linux Copy cmake --preset linux cmake --build --preset linux ctest --preset linux-debug macOS Copy cmake --preset macos cmake --build --preset macos ctest --preset macos-debug Built examples land in bin/ . Using ASGE in your own C++ project Either way, pull in the whole engine through the umbrella header: Copy #include <ASGE/ASGE.hpp> Option 1 — add_subdirectory Vendor ASGE into your project (e.g. as a submodule under third-party/asge ) and add it directly: CMakeLists.txt Copy add_subdirectory(third-party/asge) add_executable(my_game main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE ASGE) # On Windows, my_game.exe also needs SDL3.dll next to it at runtime asge_copy_sdl3_runtime(my_game) Option 2 — FetchContent CMakeLists.txt Copy include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare( asge GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/lmriccardo/a-simple-game-engine.git GIT_TAG main SOURCE_DIR "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/third-party/asge" ) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(asge) add_executable(my_game main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE ASGE) asge_copy_sdl3_runtime(my_game) ASGE's own de

title: Moving Box
text: ← All examples Rendering · Input Moving Box The smallest playable game The example linked from the project README's own quick-start: a single WASD-controlled box drawn with IRenderer::DrawRect . It's deliberately minimal — one entity, no ECS, no assets — to show the shortest path from Application<TGame> to something on screen that responds to a player. Controls W A S D Move the box Rendering Input Run it yourself build just this example Copy cmake --build --preset windows-debug --target moving_box # binary lands under bin/ (e.g. bin/Debug/moving_box.exe on Windows) See Installation for the full build setup. title: Text Rendering
text: ← All examples Rendering · Assets Text Rendering Fonts, sizes and color Bakes the same font at three different pixel heights — each ASGE Font is rasterized at one fixed size, so multiple on-screen sizes means loading it multiple times, each with its own atlas texture. A headline drawn alongside them continuously cycles through hue space, exercising per-draw color tinting on top of the baked glyph atlas. No input — purely a visual reference for this subsystem. Rendering Assets Run it yourself build just this example Copy cmake --build --preset windows-debug --target text_demo # binary lands under bin/ (e.g. bin/Debug/text_demo.exe on Windows) See Installation for the full build setup. title: Camera & Viewport

title: Camera Follow
text: ← All examples Rendering · ECS Camera Follow ECS camera-follow with off-screen culling The ECS-driven counterpart to camera_demo : a player entity ( Transform + Velocity + Camera , set as resources::ActiveCamera ) WASD-driven through a 40×30-tile world, 1280×960 — well beyond the 800×600 window. systems::CameraSystem smoothly follows the player every frame, and RenderSystem culls tiles outside the visible area ( video::VisibleWorldRect ) rather than submitting a draw call for all 1,200 of them. title: Sprite Rotation

title: Scene Management
text: ← All examples Scenes · ECS · Assets Scene Management A whole level loaded from TOML Loads its whole entity set from a hand-authored TOML scene file ( assets/scene.toml ) via SceneManager::LoadScene instead of spawning entities in code — see ecs_demo for the code-driven equivalent this replaces. Ties together every ASGE subsystem at its current state: the virtual filesystem loads the TOML, the asset pipeline resolves textures, the ECS registry holds the resulting entities, and SceneManager can swap the whole active scene at runtime or snapshot it back out to disk. title: Physics
text: ← All examples Physics · ECS Physics Gravity, collision response and triggers Showcase for Rigidbody , gravity, mass-weighted collision response, and Trigger colliders, all driven through systems::PhysicsUpdate . A floor and two side walls are static Solid Colliders — deliberately no Velocity / Rigidbody , so collision response treats them as immovable. title: Path Following
text: ← All examples Physics · ECS · Assets · Rendering Path Following A car driving a closed, curved street End-to-end showcase for components::PathFollow and systems::PathFollowingSystem : a car drives a closed, curved street loop built from math::CatmullRomSpline — 13 waypoints (the first repeated at the end, since a Catmull-Rom chain doesn't wrap on its own) resolved once at spawn time, then walked every frame at a player-adjustable speed, with the car oriented to face the road's tangent direction as it turns. The street itself is drawn straight from the car's own resolved PathFollow::m_Path — IRenderer has no curve/polygon-fill primitive, so it's painted as a dense trail of overlapping filled circles (via PointAtDistance ) with a dashed centerline, rather than needing a second, separately-authored road asset. title: Scoped Profiler
text: ← All examples Profiling · Tooling Scoped Profiler Nested scope timing Times nested code paths with PROFILE_SCOPE , showing that scopes can nest inside each other the same way a real per-frame Update() would, then prints the resulting timing tree. Profiling Tooling console example — no window, see captured output below Sample output scoped_profiler output Copy -- Summary after 5 frames -- [INFO][20:35:50.199][LogSummary] [TimingProfiler] FrameUpdate — calls: 5, avg: 29735920ns, min: 21817700ns, max: 32020400ns [INFO][20:35:50.200][LogSummary] [TimingProfiler] FastOperation — calls: 5, avg: 13886280ns, min: 6636000ns, max: 16007300ns [INFO][20:35:50.200][LogSummary] [TimingProfiler] SlowOperation — calls: 5, avg: 15843240ns, min: 15166000ns, max: 16023100ns -- Summary after ResetAll (buckets are empty, nothing logged) -- Run it yourself build just this example Copy cmake --build --preset windows-debug --target scoped_profiler # binary lands under bin/ (e.g. bin/Debug/scoped_profiler.exe on Windows) See Installation for the full build setup. Source examples/scoped_profiler/main.cpp Copy #include <chrono> #include <iostream> #include <thread> #include <ASGE/Core/Profiling/ScopedTimer.hpp> using namespace asge::profiling; namespace { void FastOperation() { PROFILE_SCOPE("FastOperation"); std::this_thread::sleep_for( std::chrono::milliseconds(1) ); } void SlowOperation() { PROFILE_SCOPE("SlowOperation"); std::this_thread::sleep_for( std::chrono::milliseconds(10) ); } void FrameUpdate() { // A scope can wrap other scopes, just like a real per-frame update would. PROFILE_SCOPE("FrameUpdate"); FastOperation(); SlowOperation(); } } int main() { constexpr int frames = 5; for ( int frame = 0; frame < frames; ++frame ) { FrameUpdate(); } std::cout << "-- Summary after " << frames << " frames --" << std::endl; TimingProfiler::Instance().LogSummary(); TimingProfiler::Instance().ResetAll(); std::cout << "-- Summary after ResetAll (buckets are empty, nothing logged) --" << std::end

title: A Simple Game Engine
text: A Simple Game Engine · ASGE ASGE Overview Engine Editor Releases GitHub Search Ctrl K Overview Engine Editor Releases GitHub MIT Licensed · C++23 · SDL3 A Simple Game Engine, built to stay out of your way. ASGE is a modular, lightweight, cross-platform 2D game engine written in modern C++ (C++23) on top of SDL3 . Small composable subsystems, an ECS-based gameplay layer, and a growing set of runnable examples — targeting Windows, Linux and macOS. Get started Browse examples API reference View on GitHub 20 runnable examples C++23 modern, header-driven API 3 target platforms SDL3 current render backend Engine Install ASGE, learn how it works, browse the API reference and runnable examples. Level editor Build projects, scenes, colliders and animations visually, then run them on the engine. Built around four ideas Performance Thin abstractions over SDL3, custom allocators, and a thread pool for concurrent work — the engine tries to stay out of your frame budget's way. Simplicity Small, composable subsystems instead of one monolithic framework. Pull in what a game needs through the ASGE.hpp umbrella header. Extensibility An ECS-based gameplay layer plus a signal/event system ( asge::signals::Signal ) for decoupling systems from each other. Tooling A debug logger, timing/profiling utilities ( ScopedTimer ), a virtual filesystem, and a growing set of runnable examples. Repository layout Path Contents src/ASGE/ Engine source — Application, Core, Events, Game, Input, Video, Audio examples/ Small standalone programs demonstrating each subsystem tests/ GoogleTest unit test suite docs/roadmap/ Design docs and the phased implementation roadmap scripts/ Dependency-fetching scripts (SDL3, stb) for each platform cmake/ CMake package config used when ASGE is installed Roadmap status ASGE is under active development, worked through a phased roadmap . Tiers are priority order; each system also has its own phase docs for scope/maturity. Tier 0 — Foundation Core Engine Done docs → Render

title: Engine theory
text: Engine theory What the main parts of a game engine do, and how ASGE implements the ones it has today. Each page first explains the concept, then shows the ASGE types that realise it. Entity-Component-System Entities, components, systems and views, and how ASGE's Registry implements them. Game loop & timing The main loop, the per-frame system order, game states, the clock and profiling. Events & signals SDL event translation, SystemEvent and the type-safe Signal/Connection pattern. Memory & threading Linear, pool and stack allocators, the free-list and the ThreadPool. Shorter overviews Input - Keyboard and mouse state tracked every frame from the event stream. Rendering - The thin video layer over SDL3: window, renderer, textures, cameras and primitives. Audio - The audio device and streams, driven by AudioSource components. title: Entity-Component-System
text: Entity-Component-System An ECS splits a game object into identity , data and behaviour , so behaviour can be written once and applied to every object that has the right data. The concept Entity - just an id. It carries no data and no code. Component - a plain bundle of data (a position, a sprite, a collider) attached to an entity. System - a function that walks every entity owning a given set of components and acts on them. Storing each component type in its own densely packed array keeps iteration cache-friendly, and composing objects from components avoids deep inheritance hierarchies. How ASGE does it Generational entity handles An asge::ecs::Entity is an index plus a generation counter. When an entity is destroyed its slot is recycled and its generation is bumped, so any stale handle still held elsewhere fails IsAlive() instead of silently pointing at an unrelated new entity. A slot whose generation reaches its maximum is retired rather than reused. Indices come from a fixed-capacity EntityAllocator built on mem::FreeList (see Memory & threading ). Sparse-set component pools Each component type lives in its own ComponentPool<T> , a sparse set: a sparse array maps an entity index to a slot in a dense array of components. Insert , Get , Remove and Contains are O(1), and iteration only touches live components. Removal is swap-and-pop, so iteration order may change after a removal. The Registry asge::ecs::Registry is the single entry point. It owns the allocator and one pool per component type, created lazily on the first AddComponent<T> . DestroyEntity() strips the entity from every pool. The registry also holds per-registry resources ( SetResource<T> / GetResource<T> ): at most one value of a type that is not tied to any entity. Views Registry::View<Ts...>() returns a lazy, non-owning View over every entity that has all of Ts . It iterates the smallest contributing pool and filters the rest. Entities carrying the Disable marker, or whose ancestor in the Hierarchy

title: Game loop & timing
text: Game loop & timing The game loop is the heartbeat of a game: read input, advance the simulation by the time that passed, draw, repeat. The concept Each iteration of the loop is a frame . Simulation code must be told how long the previous frame took (the delta time ) so movement stays the same speed on a 30 Hz and a 144 Hz display. Engines differ on whether the simulation uses a variable step (one update per frame with the real delta) or a fixed step (update at a constant rate, possibly several times per frame); a variable step is simpler, a fixed step is more deterministic. How ASGE does it Application asge::Application<TGame> owns the video, input and audio systems and constructs your TGame in place. Run() executes the loop below and stops on an OS quit event or when a game state requests TransitionKind::Quit . Application.hpp Copy // asge::Application<TGame>::Run(), abridged while ( m_Running ) { GET_TIMESYSTEM.Tick(); // advance the clock m_InputSys.NewFrame(); while ( SDL_PollEvent( &event ) ) // drain OS events processEvent( &event ); m_Game->Update( time::DeltaTime(), m_InputSys.GetState() ); m_Game->Render( m_VideoSys.GetRenderer() ); m_VideoSys.GetRenderer().Present(); } ASGE uses a variable timestep : one Update per frame, with the scaled delta time. The target frame rate comes from ApplicationConfig::s_TargetFps . One frame inside Game Game<TStateId>::Update runs the systems in the only valid order: UI interaction the active state's own Update() (your game logic) - states never call systems themselves gravity, movement, path following UI layout, then one transform propagation collision detection and resolution, then trigger events audio Render then resolves pending assets, clears with the visible state's colour, draws the scene through the render pipeline, and finally lets the states draw on top. Game states Screens are IGameState objects on a GameStateStack . A state's Update may return a Transition to Push , Pop , Replace or Quit . Your Game subclass imp

title: Events & signals
text: Events & signals Decoupled communication lets one part of the program announce that something happened without knowing who cares. The concept Two common patterns: an event stream , where the platform produces a sequence of typed messages that code polls or receives, and signals and slots , where a producer exposes a typed signal and any number of listeners (slots) connect callbacks to it. Both remove direct dependencies between the sender and its receivers. How ASGE does it System events SDL events are translated once, in event::_internal::ProcessEvent , into asge::event::SystemEvent : a std::variant over QuitEvent , WindowEvent , KeyboardEvent , MouseMotionEvent , MouseButtonEvent , MouseWheelEvent and UnknownEvent . Game code never sees SDL types; it asks for the case it cares about with TryGet<EventT>() , which returns a pointer or null. Application forwards each event to the input system and then to Game::OnSystemEvent . state.cpp Copy void OnSystemEvent( asge::event::SystemEvent const& inSysEvent ) override { if ( auto const* key = inSysEvent.TryGet<asge::event::KeyboardEvent>() ) { // react to the key press } } Signals asge::signals::Signal<Args...> is a thread-safe, type-checked signal: every slot must have the signature of the signal. Connect() returns a Connection . A connection ends when you call Disconnect() or when the optional lifetime token (a weak pointer you pass to Connect() ) expires. Dead connections are pruned automatically on the next Emit() . signals.cpp Copy asge::signals::Signal<int> onScore; // Slot signature must match the signal's: void(int) auto connection = onScore.Connect( []( int points ) { /* update HUD */ } ); onScore.Emit( 10 ); // runs every connected slot connection.Disconnect(); // or pass a lifetime token to Connect() for automatic cleanup Choosing System events carry what the OS reports; signals are for your own code, for example a gameplay system announcing a score change to the HUD. See also Source: Events/Events.hpp , Core/P

title: Memory & threading
text: Memory & threading Games allocate and free a lot of small things every frame; predictable allocation and safe parallel work keep the frame time steady. The concept General-purpose new / delete can be slow and fragment memory. Game engines replace it, where it matters, with allocators that match an allocation pattern : bump pointers for per-frame scratch data, pools for many same-sized objects, stacks for strictly nested lifetimes. For CPU parallelism, a thread pool reuses a fixed set of worker threads instead of spawning one per task. How ASGE does it Allocators ( asge::mem ) Type Pattern Notes LinearAllocator Arena / bump pointer O(1) alloc over a buffer you provide; Reset() frees everything, GetMarker() + Rewind() roll back; no individual frees. PoolAllocator<T, N> Fixed-size slots O(1) alloc and free from a free-list; returns an owning pointer whose deleter gives the slot back. Created through Create() as a shared_ptr . StackAllocator<N> LIFO Frees must be in reverse order (asserted in debug); GetMarker() / FreeToMarker() unwind and run destructors. FreeList<N> Index allocator Hands out indices in [0, N) with double-free detection. The ECS uses it to issue entity indices. Thread pool ( asge::concurrent ) ThreadPool owns a fixed set of Worker threads and a shared lock-free queue. Submit() wraps a callable and its arguments in a job and returns a std::future<T> , or nothing for a callable that returns void . The pool is neither copyable nor movable because workers hold references to its queue. threads.cpp Copy asge::concurrent::ThreadPool pool; // defaults to the hardware concurrency auto result = pool.Submit( []( int n ) { return n * 2; }, 21 ); // std::future<int> int value = result.get(); // 42 pool.Submit( [] { /* void work: no future is returned */ } ); See also Source: Core/Memory/ , Core/Concurrent/ThreadPool.hpp . ECS shows the free-list in use.
